searchText: Think the flashbot GitHub should have good resources. Hasu from paradigm has good writings/talks on the topic as well as you pointed out w/ uncommon core Perhaps yet another dumber question than the one first asked by <@427013411004612618> — why is MEV a problem at all? Is MEV that much of a deadweight loss to the system vs being a source of revenue capture to allow block proposers to operate profitably, thereby being part of the “necessary” security budget of ethereum? To use the “ethereum is a nation-state” analogy, I’d rather have a well-funded defense budget that is deployed in the best interests of the commonwealth but have a little bit of “corruption” than a squeaky clean one that is ineffective and would need to be funded with seigniorage One issue is that capturing MEV creates negative externalities / degrades throughput, and another is that MEV can lead to consensus instability (reorgs at a minimum degrade UX of accepting payments, and be even nastier). Consider a humble sandwich attack: a single Uniswap tx that consumes about 105,000 gas leads to another transaction on either side. Now there's 315,000 gas consumed for the utility of a single person swapping, at the expense of the primary swapper. (there are 'triple stacked sandwiches' with three 'authentic' tx with the two MEV-capture tx (the bread) on either side, but these are far rarer than the single-stacked, humble sandwich). Thanks that’s helpful. Yeah agree sandwich attacks / MEV in general seems to be a “non-productive” use of gas (could make a similar claim in tradfi about usage of bandwidth for HFT / algo hedge funds which is probably the right analogy here). That said, it seems like explicitly tagged “MEV bots” actually account for a very small portion of gas used per this: https://ultrasound.money/ I wonder if anyone has done a study / crunched the data on how much more incremental slippage MEV causes on DEXs or how much of the total gas usage around DeFi-specifically (not sure how MEV works in the context of NFTs for example?) comes from productive activities vs MEV Hey. I want to get into blockchain development on ethereum. I am fully fluent in python and above average in java. Can someone suggest me a path from where I can begin the blockchain development? I'm waiting on actual Yakuza MEV. ETH organizations like exchanges paying protection fees to ensure their stuff is included or paying mercenary fees to ensure their competitions transactions are excluded. There's a lot of real world examples of practices that were banned that haven't been tried yet. I'm not well read on HFT, but I think there are claims that liquidity commands a premium: if a stock trades close to the stock exchange's tick size then the market might function worse / be less efficient (e.g. respondant to information). Share splits / redomination shouldn't add value (outside of the psychological) except in unit issues like this. There are other arguments for the value of liquidity, so at least HFT provides some positive externality. If miners took smaller cuts from Flashbots Searchers, then DEX prices might be a little better, since they'd accept making smaller arbitrages than they do now. Do Ethermine reorgs come close enough? I’ll admit my ignorance there. They don’t have enough hashrate to reorganize eth I think? check the pinned post at <#745072678079168654> Assuming they have 25-35% hashrate, they'd be able to pull off short-term reorgs with decent probability. If the MEV eclipses the tx fees it could be worth risking. https://miningpoolstats.stream/ethereum places them at 32%, and miningpools.com/ethereum/ places them at 27%. I'm not sure about my statements here though.

excerpts.content:
Perhaps yet another dumber question than the one first asked by <@427013411004612618> — why is MEV a problem at all? Is MEV that much of a deadweight loss to the system vs being a source of revenue capture to allow block proposers to operate profitably, thereby being part of the “necessary” security budget of ethereum?

To use the “ethereum is a nation-state” analogy, I’d rather have a well-funded defense budget that is deployed in the best interests of the commonwealth but have a little bit of “corruption” than a squeaky clean one that is ineffective and would need to be funded with seigniorage

excerpts.author: 3xmd1559sporebraytondingo
excerpts.content:
One issue is that capturing MEV creates negative externalities / degrades throughput, and another is that MEV can lead to consensus instability (reorgs at a minimum degrade UX of accepting payments, and be even nastier). 

Consider a humble sandwich attack: a single Uniswap tx that consumes about 105,000 gas leads to another transaction on either side. Now there's 315,000 gas consumed for the utility of a single person swapping, at the expense of the primary swapper.

(there are 'triple stacked sandwiches' with three 'authentic' tx with the two MEV-capture tx (the bread) on either side, but these are far rarer than the single-stacked, humble sandwich).

excerpts.author: randomishwalk
excerpts.content:
Thanks that’s helpful. Yeah agree sandwich attacks / MEV in general seems to be a “non-productive” use of gas (could make a similar claim in tradfi about usage of bandwidth for HFT / algo hedge funds which is probably the right analogy here). 

That said, it seems like explicitly tagged “MEV bots” actually account for a very small portion of gas used per this: https://ultrasound.money/

I wonder if anyone has done a study / crunched the data on how much more incremental slippage MEV causes on DEXs or how much of the total gas usage around DeFi-specifically (not sure how MEV works in the context of NFTs for example?) comes from productive activities vs MEV
